chief_complaint: painful red skin with blisters on hand post-hot oil
hpi_details: A 77-year-old male presents to the clinic with painful, red, blistered skin on his hand after hot oil splashed on it earlier today. The pain has been constant since the injury occurred.
ideas: thinks it might be related to burn
concerns: worried about potential complications and long term recovery
expectations: wants complete diagnostic evaluation and treatment plan

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Second-Degree (Partial-Thickness) Burn is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management for Second-Degree (Partial-Thickness) Burn emphasizes cooling and gentle cleansing, a non-adherent dressing with adequate analgesia (avoiding routine silver sulfadiazine, which can delay healing of superficial partial-thickness burns), and prompt referral for hand burns, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: painful red skin with blisters on hand post-hot oil
Key HPI features: A 77-year-old male presents with painful, red, blistered skin on his hand after hot oil splashed on it earlier today; the pain has been constant since the injury occurred.
Objective/Exam findings: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Second-Degree Burn hand.
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Second-Degree (Partial-Thickness) Burn.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to First-degree (superficial) burn without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Burn covering a large body surface area or involving the face/airway.
management_principles: Plan for Second-Degree Burn hand: Cool and cleanse the wound, apply a non-adherent dressing with analgesia (avoid routine silver sulfadiazine, which can delay healing), refer promptly for hand-burn assessment
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of painful red skin with blisters on hand post-hot oil, consistent with a partial-thickness thermal injury.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Second-Degree Burn hand.
reference_soap.assessment: Assessment consistent with Second-Degree (Partial-Thickness) Burn of the hand.
reference_soap.plan: Cool with running water if promptly after injury, cleanse gently, remove constricting items, and use a nonadherent dressing with appropriate analgesia. Avoid routine silver sulfadiazine for superficial partial-thickness burns because it can delay healing. Refer promptly for burn/hand assessment because the burn involves the hand.

teaching.one_liner: A partial-thickness thermal injury damaging the epidermis and part of the dermis, causing painful, red, blistered skin.
red_flags: Burn covering a large body surface area or involving the face/airway
Signs of infection (spreading redness, pus, fever)

must_ask.say: What caused the burn, and when did it happen?
How large is the burned area, and are there blisters?
How painful is it right now?
Did you cool it with water, and have you put anything on it?
Any increasing redness, pus, or fever since it happened?
